task.title: Font selection and sizing
task.shortdesc: Font declarations choose a family, a size and a face within that family. They can also control line spacing and whether the processor may create a style that the font does not contain. Put declarations inside a rule that selects the XML elements you want to style:

context.p: For variant and OpenType feature properties, see Font variants and features. For variable fonts and color palettes, see Variable and color fonts.

step.cmd: Choosing the font family and size

info.p: CSS Fonts 4 §2.1, Font family: the font-family property; CSS Fonts 4 §2.1.5, Generic font families.

Use font-family to name the typeface family. Separate alternatives with commas. Put a family name containing spaces in quotes. If a family is unavailable or cannot provide a character, the processor can try the next family in the list.

stepxmp.pre: body { font-family: "Noto Serif", "Times New Roman", serif; }

info.p: The final serif is a generic family name. It describes a broad typeface style rather than naming a font file. Other generic names include sans-serif and monospace. Available family names depend on the fonts CSSMedia can access.
ISO 32000-1 §9.6.2, Standard Type 1 Fonts.
PDF defines 14 standard typefaces. They are grouped here by design and face:

ul.li: The Times faces have serifs. The Helvetica faces do not. The Courier faces use fixed-width advances, so each glyph occupies the same width.
Symbol contains a symbol character set. ZapfDingbats contains ornamental marks and symbols.

In each four-face group, Bold identifies the heavier face, Italic the italic face, and Oblique the slanted face. Times-BoldItalic combines bold and italic; Helvetica-BoldOblique and Courier-BoldOblique combine bold and oblique.

CSSMedia includes these standard font faces as font data. Its built-in fallback for the generic family serif uses the four Times faces, sans-serif uses the four Helvetica faces, and monospace uses the four Courier faces.

CSS family lookup also includes the standard groups Times, Helvetica, Courier, Symbol and ZapfDingbats. The generic keywords describe broad typographic categories; the standard group names identify the bundled font families.

info.p: CSS Fonts 4 §2.5, Font size: the font-size property.
Use font-size to set the size of text. You can use a length such as 12pt, a percentage, a relative keyword such as larger, or a length relative to another font size.
An em value is based on the font size inherited by the selected element. A percentage is based on the parent element’s font size. Use a length such as pt when you want to state an explicit size.
CSS Fonts 5 §3.4, Relative sizing: the font-size-adjust property.

Use font-size-adjust to request a consistent size for a chosen font measurement, such as the height of lowercase letters. This can help keep text visually similar when the preferred font is unavailable and a fallback font has different proportions.
The property can use a metric name such as ex-height or cap-height, followed by a number, or from-font to use the metric from the font.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.2, Font weight: the font-weight property.
Use font-weight to choose how heavy the letters look. The common values are normal and bold. You can also use a number from 1 to 1000. In the usual scale, 400 is normal and 700 is bold.
The values bolder and lighter choose a weight relative to the inherited weight. A font family may not contain every requested weight. CSSMedia uses this property when matching an available font face.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.3, Font width: the font-width property.
Use font-width to request narrower or wider letters. You can use a percentage or a keyword from ultra-condensed through ultra-expanded.
The older name font-stretch is accepted by CSSMedia as an alias for font-width. A font family may not provide every width. CSSMedia uses the requested width when matching a font face.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.4, Font style: the font-style property.
Use font-style to request upright or slanted letters. The usual values are normal, italic and oblique.

stepxmp.pre: body { font-style: normal; } em { font-style: italic; }

info.p: An oblique value can include an angle. The specification also defines left and right oblique directions. A font family may not contain a face for every style. CSSMedia uses this property when matching a font face.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.8, Controlling synthetic faces.

If a font family does not contain a requested face, a processor may create a synthetic version, such as making regular letters look heavier. Use font-synthesis to allow or disable these substitutions.

none disables synthetic weight, style, small-caps and subscript or superscript faces. The keyword weight, style, small-caps or position allows that kind of synthesis. The longhand properties control those choices separately.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.8.1, Controlling synthesized bold: The font-synthesis-weight property.
This property controls whether the processor may make a font look heavier when the family lacks the requested weight. Use none to forbid that synthetic bolding, or auto to allow it.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.8.2, Controlling synthesized oblique: The font-synthesis-style property.

This property controls whether the processor may slant a font when the family lacks the requested italic or oblique face. Use none to forbid a synthetic slant. oblique-only allows synthesis for oblique styles but not italic styles. auto allows the normal synthesis behavior.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.8.3, Controlling synthesized small caps: The font-synthesis-small-caps property.
This property controls whether the processor may create small capitals when the font does not provide them. Use none to forbid synthetic small capitals, or auto to allow them.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.8.4, Controlling synthesized super- and subscripts: The font-synthesis-position property.
This property controls whether the processor may create subscript or superscript forms when the font does not provide them. Use none to forbid those synthetic forms, or auto to allow them.
CSS Fonts 4 §2.7, Shorthand font property: the font property.

Use font to set several font properties in one declaration. Write optional style, variant, weight and width values first. Then write the required size, an optional slash and line height, and the required family.

stepxmp.pre: chapter { font: italic bold 12pt/1.4 "Noto Serif", serif; }

info.p: The size and family are required. The shorthand also accepts system font keywords such as caption and menu. It resets other properties in the shorthand to their initial values. Use separate declarations when you want to set advanced font features without resetting them.

CSS Fonts 4 allows a user agent to substitute its default font when the requested system font is unavailable. CSSMedia uses the system-ui family and initial values for the other font subproperties as that fallback. It does not resolve platform-specific settings for roles such as caption or menu.
CSS Inline Layout 3 §5.1, Line Spacing: the line-height property.

Use line-height to control the height of a line of text. A unitless number multiplies the font size. A length states the line height directly. A percentage is relative to the font size. normal lets the processor choose a value.
With a font size of 12pt, line-height: 1.4 requests a line height of 1.4 times the font size. A unitless number scales when the font size changes.
